5            Conclusion and Limitations

MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs fail for structural reasons: the normalization needed
for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs. Raw pre-
normalization routing fixes the failure and motivates Residual-IA+ ; R(D) identifies where it applies.


Implication. Routing collapse on instance-normalized backbones generalizes a broader pattern:
when a foundation model’s input pipeline destroys signal that a downstream router needs, optimization-
side rescues (load balancing, z-loss, ReLU routing) cannot recover what is structurally absent. The
fix is to restore the missing input, not to retune the optimizer. The same mechanism arises in
vision (Appendix H.1) and predicts where future MoE-on-FM systems will and will not benefit from
raw-signal access.


Limitations. Three boundaries scope our claims. (i) Normalization specificity. Our diagnosis
applies to backbones with instance-level normalization (RevIN, BatchNorm, GroupNorm); backbones
without it (Chronos, Timer-XL) show no collapse and no RR-MoA gain, as Observation 1 predicts.
Extensions to attention-based or learned normalizers are not characterized. (ii) Signal-ratio boundary
cases. The signal-ratio predictor R(D) is a single monotone proxy for variance contribution; on
Solar (R=0.06) it correctly flags low benefit but is not sharp. Datasets with strong shape-statistics
coupling fall outside the tight regime of the bound. (iii) Forecasting and imputation only. We
evaluate forecasting and imputation on LTSF benchmarks. Anomaly detection, classification, and
irregularly-sampled tasks are deferred to future work.

            loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recovers at most 10.9%

            decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor of when collapse matters (Spear-

            should not help. The fix follows: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)
            routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA wins 54/54 dataset/freeze-

1972	\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
1973	\label{app:deployment}
1974	
1975	The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
1976	
1977	\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds.
